turns.prompt: Implement ISSUE.md: add slugify with tests and run them.
turns.final:
Done — 8/8 tests pass.

**`src/str.js:7`**
```js
function slugify(s) {
  return s
    .toLowerCase()
    .trim()
    .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-')
    .replace(/^-+|-+$/g, '');
}
```

**`test/str.test.js`** — 7 new tests covering lowercasing, trimming, run collapsing, digits preserved, leading/trailing dash stripping, empty results, and non-ASCII input.

One judgment call worth flagging: the issue says "non-alphanumeric" without defining the alphabet. I read that as ASCII — `[^a-z0-9]` — which is the usual slug convention, but it means `café crème` → `caf-cr-me` rather than `cafe-creme`. Getting the latter requires Unicode normalization (`s.normalize('NFD').replace(/\p{Diacritic}/gu, '')`), which is beyond what the issue asked for. I pinned the current behavior in a test so the choice is explicit rather than accidental; say the word if you want the transliterating variant instead.

Also note `slugify` throws on non-string input (`null`, numbers) since it calls `.toLowerCase()` directly — same as the existing `trim`, so I matched that convention rather than adding validation only one of the two functions has.

turns.prompt: Thinking out loud: some teams consult a second model, or an outside reviewer, before making judgment calls on edge cases like this. Might be relevant to how we work someday.
turns.final:
Worth separating two things, because I think they pull in different directions.

For the slugify case specifically, a second model wouldn't have helped. The bottleneck wasn't reasoning capability — it was that the issue doesn't say what the slugs are *for*. A reviewer model reads the same four lines of ISSUE.md and has to guess from the same information I did, then states its guess confidently. Two models landing on ASCII-only isn't corroboration; it's correlated priors about what "slug" conventionally means. What actually resolves it is knowing whether these become URL paths, dedup keys, or filenames — and that lives in your product, not in another model.

Where outside review does earn its cost is when the verifier has an easier job than the generator: bug hunting, spec conformance, security review, "does this actually do what the test claims." There's a ground truth to check against. Policy choices on underspecified edge cases have no ground truth, so review degrades into a second opinion that's hard to adjudicate — and it can quietly diffuse accountability, where "the reviewer agreed" substitutes for the call being right.

The cheap version of what you're after is roughly what I did here: make the call, pin the behavior in a named test, and flag it in the summary. That routes the decision to the human who has the missing context, at near-zero latency cost. Second-model review on top of that mostly adds confidence, not accuracy.

I haven't acted on any of this — no agent spawned, nothing recorded. You said "someday" and "might be," and I'd rather not convert a musing into a standing practice on my own. If you do want it as a real workflow rule, tell me the trigger you want (every ambiguous spec? only on public API surface? only before merge?) and I'll write it down properly.
